Subject: Scheduling memo — Multi‑mode, resource‑constrained project with budget and timing limits

Overview
We are planning and sequencing a set of interrelated activities that must share limited renewable resources while operating under a fixed budget and explicit timing requirements. Each activity can be executed in one of several modes, and the chosen mode determines how long the activity takes, how much of each shared resource it consumes while it runs, and how much it costs. Our aim is to select a single mode for each activity and set start times so that all dependencies and timing rules are respected, resources are used safely, spending stays within the project budget, and the overall completion time is minimized.

Execution modes and trade‑offs
- Each activity has multiple execution options. Faster modes shorten the schedule but typically consume more resources and cost more. Slower modes may be cheaper and lighter on resources, but they extend the activity’s run time.
- Once a mode is selected for an activity, it runs without interruption until completion (no preemption).
- The sum of the costs for the chosen modes must remain within the project’s fixed budget.

Dependencies and timing controls
- The work is governed by precedence links: certain activities cannot start until their predecessors finish.
- Some dependencies include minimum delays (the successor must wait at least a stated amount of time after the predecessor finishes) and, in some cases, maximum delays (the successor must start within a set window after the predecessor finishes).
- A subset of activities has earliest allowed start times, and some have hard completion deadlines that must not be violated.

Renewable resources and the conservative safety rule
- We have multiple types of renewable resources with fixed capacities. When an activity finishes, any resources it used return to the shared pool.
- To guard against potential overloads without live, moment‑to‑moment metering, we apply a conservative, pairwise safety rule for activities that are not linked by precedence:
  • If there exists even one combination of their execution modes and one resource type for which their combined usage would exceed that resource’s capacity, those two activities must not overlap. They must be sequenced so that one finishes before the other starts.
  • If no such overload risk exists for any mode pairing and resource, the activities may overlap (subject to all other dependencies and timing rules).
- This pairwise rule is the only resource capacity mechanism we apply; there is no separate, continuous capacity check beyond these sequencing decisions.

Budget discipline
- The project operates under a fixed, non‑renewable budget. The total cost of the selected modes across all activities must not exceed this cap.
- Choosing faster modes can accelerate completion but may require reallocating budget from other activities or accepting additional sequencing constraints due to higher potential resource draws.

Scheduling goal and implications
- Goal: Minimize the overall project duration while meeting all dependency, timing, resource, and budget requirements.
- Practical implications:
  • Mode choices interact with the safety rule. Selecting higher‑consumption modes can force additional activity sequencing and reduce parallelism. Conversely, lighter modes may permit more concurrent work but extend individual task durations.
  • Precedence links with minimum and maximum delays, along with release dates and deadlines, further constrain feasible start times, requiring careful coordination of handoffs and windows.
  • Because activities cannot be interrupted once started, start times should be set to ensure that resources, lags, and due dates are satisfied throughout each activity’s full duration.

Next steps
- Confirm the activity list, execution modes, resource capacities, dependencies and lags, release dates, and deadlines.
- Evaluate mode combinations and apply the pairwise safety rule to identify mandatory sequencing decisions between otherwise independent activities.
- Build a baseline schedule that meets the budget cap and timing requirements, then iterate on mode selections to compress the makespan where cost and resource safety allow.
